newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP pressures Waigel with no-go tax stance.
newsitem.headline: German FDP pressures Waigel with no-go tax stance.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), junior partners in the coalition government, piled pressure on Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday by insisting they would not let taxes rise to plug a huge budget gap.

The issue has begun to strain Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition as Waigel scrambles for funds to make up a huge revenue shortfall, and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) push for higher taxes to help Germany meet the criteria for Europe's planned single currency.
FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt was quoted on Monday as saying the party would not let the 1998 budget include tax increases.
"We are not going to wobble on this," he told the Bild newspaper, according to an advance release of Tuesday's edition.

Media reports said Kohl's CDU and its sister party, Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU), are losing patience with the FDP and said if it did not agree to higher fuel or value-added tax, a planned cut in the so-called solidarity tax agreed with the FDP should be postponed.
This would be a blow to the FDP, which has practically staked its survival on its determination to cut taxes.
But it would also be a risky move for Kohl, who might endanger the FDP's chance of returning to parliament in the September 1998 election, and so be left without a majority.
Gerhardt insisted that the cut in the solidarity tax, which goes to pay for east German economic restructuring, had been "firmly agreed in the coalition" and would go ahead as planned.
But he also said he did not expect the issue to threaten the survival of the coalition, with its slim 12-seat majority.
"I can't see that happening. I don't set much store by threats," he said.
The CDU and CSU have been reluctant to put too much pressure on the FDP before the liberal party holds a national conference next weekend.
But FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle insisted to Hesse state television that the FDP would not agree to tax rises, "even after the party conference".

The issue has become urgent since an expert commission said last week tax revenues would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) below budget this year, and could be another 32 billion marks short of the government forecast next year.

Bonn has committed itself so strongly to iron budget discipline for itself and its European Union partners that letting its deficit rise above the limit set to qualify for monetary union to start in 1999 is almost unthinkable.

Waigel immediately began to sound out last-resort methods for raising money, such as revaluing central bank gold reserves and selling shareholdings, prompting the scorn of a host of economic experts who said he was undermining Germany's hard-earned credibility.
Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister warned the government in a speech to bankers in Buenos Aires on Monday not to gamble with its credibility.

"Measures which only have a short-term effect to window dress the financial situation, or even pure accounting tricks which shift part of the deficit into the future, not only lead to a loss of confidence on financial markets and among the public," he said.
"They would also become transparent soon after the start of monetary union," he said.
